title: start() vs run() — calling run() directly does NOT create a new thread
shortTitle: start() vs run() — calling run() directly does NOT create a new thread

s1_definition.profdef: `start()` creates a NEW OS thread, then the JVM calls `run()` on that new thread. The caller continues in parallel — true multithreading. `run()` called directly is just a NORMAL METHOD CALL on the CURRENT thread — no new thread is created, no parallelism, no concurrency. It executes sequentially like any other method. This is one of the most common beginner mistakes: calling `thread.run()` instead of `thread.start()` and wondering why code isn't running in parallel. `start()` can only be called ONCE — calling it twice throws `IllegalThreadStateException`.
s1_definition.analogy: `start()` = hiring a NEW teller and telling them "go serve customers at your counter" — the new teller works IN PARALLEL with you. Both of you serve customers simultaneously. `run()` = you YOURSELF do the teller's job at THEIR counter — you leave YOUR counter, go to their counter, do the work, come back. No new teller hired. No parallelism. You just did extra work sequentially.
s1_definition.oneliner: start() = new OS thread + calls run() on it (parallel). run() directly = no new thread, just a method call on current thread (sequential). ALWAYS use start(), NEVER call run() directly.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `start()` creates a NEW OS thread, then the JVM calls `run()` on that new thread. The caller continues in parallel — true multithreading. `run()` called directly is just a NORMAL METHOD CALL on the CURRENT thread — no new thread is created, no parallelism, no concurrency. It executes sequentially like any other method. This is one of the most common beginner mistakes: calling `thread.run()` instead of `thread.start()` and wondering why code isn't running in parallel. `start()` can only be called ONCE — calling it twice throws `IllegalThreadStateException`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** `start()` = hiring a NEW teller and telling them "go serve customers at your counter" — the new teller works IN PARALLEL with you. Both of you serve customers simultaneously. `run()` = you YOURSELF do the teller's job at THEIR counter — you leave YOUR counter, go to their counter, do the work, come back. No new teller hired. No parallelism. You just did extra work sequentially.

**One line to remember:** start() = new OS thread + calls run() on it (parallel). run() directly = no new thread, just a method call on current thread (sequential). ALWAYS use start(), NEVER call run() directly.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — A developer wrote a batch trade processor that called `tradeThread.run()` instead of `tradeThread.start()`.** Expected: 10 trade batches processed in PARALLEL (~100ms total). Actual: 10 batches processed SEQUENTIALLY (~1000ms total). The batch ran on the main thread — no parallelism. Thread dump showed only ONE thread doing all the work. Fix: changed `run()` to `start()`. 10x faster.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** `new Thread(task)` creates a Thread object in the heap. State = NEW. No OS thread exists yet.

**Step 2a (start).** `t.start()` → JVM calls native `start0()` → OS creates a new thread → new thread calls `t.run()` → task executes on the NEW thread. Main thread continues immediately — PARALLEL.

**Step 2b (run).** `t.run()` → Java calls the `run()` method directly on the CURRENT thread → task executes on the MAIN thread. Main thread is BLOCKED until run() finishes — SEQUENTIAL.

**Step 3.** With start(): 3 threads sleeping 100ms each → all sleep in PARALLEL → total ~100ms. With run(): 3 sequential sleeps → total ~300ms.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ start() — NEW THREAD (parallel) ═══

  Main thread: ──start()──→ continues immediately ──→ ...
                    │
                    └──→ NEW Thread-0: ──run()──→ task executes ──→ terminates
  Both run simultaneously!

  ═══ run() — SAME THREAD (sequential) ═══

  Main thread: ──run()──→ task executes ──→ returns ──→ continues
  NO new thread! Main thread does ALL the work!

  ═══ TIMING PROOF ═══
  3 × start() + sleep(100ms each): ~100ms total (parallel!)
  3 × run()   + sleep(100ms each): ~300ms total (sequential!)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Thread.start() vs Thread.run() ═══

  ┌───────────────────────────────────┐
  │           Thread                   │
  │  ──────────────────────────────── │
  │  - target: Runnable               │
  │  - threadStatus: int (state)      │
  │  - name: String                   │
  │  ──────────────────────────────── │
  │  + start(): void                  │
  │    1. if state != NEW → throw ISE │
  │    2. group.add(this)             │
  │    3. start0() (native)           │  ← OS creates thread
  │       → OS thread calls run()    │
  │    4. caller returns immediately  │  ← parallel!
  │                                    │
  │  + run(): void                    │
  │    if (target != null)            │
  │      target.run();                │  ← just a method call
  │    // runs on CALLER's thread     │  ← sequential!
  └───────────────────────────────────┘

  start() call chain:
  1. Java: thread.start()
  2. JVM:  start0() (native method)
  3. OS:   pthread_create() / CreateThread()
  4. New OS thread → calls Thread.run()
  5. run() calls target.run() (the Runnable)
  6. target.run() completes → thread state = TERMINATED
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
`start()` creates a new OS thread and calls `run()` on that new thread — the caller continues immediately, enabling true parallel execution. `run()` called directly is just a regular method call on the current thread — no new thread, no parallelism, no concurrency. This is one of the most common multithreading bugs: calling `run()` instead of `start()` and getting sequential execution instead of parallel.

Internally, `start()` checks the thread state (must be NEW), then calls native `start0()` which creates a real OS thread (via `pthread_create` on Linux, `CreateThread` on Windows). The new OS thread then invokes `run()`. `start()` can only be called once — calling it on a RUNNABLE or TERMINATED thread throws `IllegalThreadStateException`. In banking: a batch processor calling `run()` instead of `start()` processed 10 trade batches sequentially in 1000ms instead of in parallel in 100ms — a 10x performance regression caused by a one-character bug (missing "start" → "run").
